Assessment adjusted with Beige Book context:
- The April 29, 2020 FOMC statement is clearly negative on growth, employment, and inflation, holding rates at the ELB and committing to continued Treasury and agency MBS/CMBS purchases to support market functioning and credit transmission.
- The Beige Book references point to broad-based stress across districts in March–April: consumer spending pressures at auto dealers and general retailers; severe strain in tourism-related employment; and manufacturing weighed by trade-related uncertainty. While some input costs (freight, metals, tariffs, natural gas) can influence prices, muted demand alongside significantly lower oil prices implies subdued inflation pressures, consistent with the FOMC’s language. Earlier reports of skilled-labor shortages and wage pressures are being overshadowed by the surge in job losses.
- SLOOS evidence of widespread tightening in C&I, CRE, and HELOCs, wider spreads, and weaker demand reinforces impaired credit flows and suggests persistent headwinds despite policy backstops.

Net effect: Beige Book sectoral and district-wide weakness, together with tighter bank lending standards, warrants a modestly more negative stance than the FOMC statement alone.
